displayedInputs.question: What characterizes the values of a discrete random variable?

choices.A: It can take every real number in an interval
choices.B: It cannot be represented by numbers
choices.D: It takes only finitely many values or values that can be listed one by one

displayedInputs.question: Toss a fair coin \(2\) times, and let \(X\) denote the number of heads. How many distinct possible values does \(X\) have?

\(X\) takes the values \(1\), \(2\), and \(3\). Given \(P(X=1)=1/2\) and \(P(X=2)=1/3\), what is \(P(X=3)\)?
\(X\) takes only the values \(0\) and \(1\), with \(P(X=0)=1/4\). What is \(P(X=1)\)?
What conditions must a probability distribution table satisfy?

choices.B: Every probability is at least \(0\), and all probabilities sum to \(1\)
choices.C: The sum of the probabilities equals the number of values
choices.D: Probabilities can be negative as long as they sum to \(1\)

displayedInputs.question: \(P(X=0)=1/5\) and \(P(X=1)=4/5\). What is the sum of these two probabilities?
The only possible values of \(X\) are 0 and 1, with \(P(X=1)=1/4\). What is \(P(X=0)\)?
In a two-point distribution, \(P(X=1)=1/4\). What is the mean of \(X\)?
What is a two-point distribution used to describe?

choices.A: A single trial has infinitely many outcomes
choices.B: The trial must be performed \(n\) times in succession
choices.C: A single trial has only two outcomes: success and failure
choices.D: The values can be any integers

displayedInputs.question: Record heads as \(1\) and tails as \(0\) for a fair coin. What is \(P(X=1)\)?
\(X\) takes the values \(1\), \(2\), and \(3\) with probabilities \(1/2\), \(1/3\), and \(1/6\), respectively. What is the mean of \(X\)?
\(X\) takes the values \(0\) and \(1\) with probabilities \(3/4\) and \(1/4\), respectively. What is the mean?
How are the values of a discrete random variable averaged to obtain its mean?

choices.B: Take only the value with the highest probability
choices.C: Divide the maximum value by the number of values
choices.D: Use the probabilities as weights and add the weighted values

displayedInputs.question: \(X\) takes the values \(2\) and \(4\), each with probability \(1/2\). What is the mean?
\(X\) takes the values \(0\) and \(1\), each with probability \(1/2\). What is the variance?
$X$ takes the values 1 and 3, each with probability $1/2$. What is the variance?
What does variance describe?

choices.A: The spread of the values relative to the mean

displayedInputs.question: $X$ always takes the value 5, that is, $P(X=5)=1$. What is the variance?
The probability of success on each trial is $1/5$, and the trials are independent. What is the probability of failure?
What conditions must Bernoulli trials satisfy?

choices.A: Each trial has only two outcomes, the probability of success is constant, and the trials are independent
choices.B: Each trial can have many outcomes
choices.C: The probability of success increases with each trial
choices.D: The outcomes of the trials must combine in a mutually exclusive way into a single outcome

displayedInputs.question: The same experiment is independently repeated 4 times. What is the number of trials $n$?
$n=3$, and the probability of success on each trial is $p=1/2$. What is the probability of failure on a single trial?
$X$ follows $B(4,1/2)$. What is $P(X=2)$?
$X$ follows $B(3,1/3)$. What is $P(X=0)$?
$X$ follows $B(2,1/2)$. What is $P(X=1)$?
What does $X$ represent in the binomial distribution $B(n,p)$?

choices.A: The probability of success on each trial
choices.B: The number of values when a trial fails
choices.C: The total number of outcomes in the sample space
choices.D: The number of successes in $n$ independent repeated trials

displayedInputs.question: $X$ follows $B(10,1/5)$. What is the mean?
$X$ follows $B(10,1/5)$. What is the variance?
$X$ follows $B(4,1/2)$. What is the mean?
Which is the formula for the variance of a binomial distribution?
Of 10 products, 4 are defective. If 3 are drawn without replacement, what is the probability that exactly 1 is defective?
Of 10 products, 4 are defective. If 3 are drawn without replacement, what is the probability that all 3 are defective?
Of 10 products, 4 are defective. If 3 are drawn without replacement, what is the probability that none are defective?
How do the sampling methods for the hypergeometric and binomial distributions differ?

choices.A: The hypergeometric distribution involves replacement after every draw
choices.B: The hypergeometric distribution involves sampling without replacement
choices.D: The hypergeometric distribution cannot use combinations

displayedInputs.question: A population contains 10 items, of which 4 belong to a specified category. If 3 items are drawn without replacement, what is the mean number of items drawn from the specified category?
A population contains 8 items, including 2 in a specified category. Draw 4 items without replacement. What is the mean?
In the hypergeometric mean formula \(nK/N\), what does \(K\) represent?

choices.B: The number of items in the specified category in the population
choices.C: The number of items in the population
choices.D: The number of items remaining after the draw
